newsitem.title: UGANDA: Ugandan traders defy order to return to work.
newsitem.headline: Ugandan traders defy order to return to work.

text.p: Ugandan traders defied an order by President Yoweri Museveni to reopen their shops on Friday and end a five-day strike that has paralysed business nationwide.
Shops remained closed in the capital Kampala where armed police patrolled the deserted streets. Reporters said traders in the other key towns stayed away as well.
Museveni ordered the traders back to work late on Thursday, threatening to cancel licences of those that defied his order.
"Those traders that continue with the strike will have their licences revoked," Museveni said in remarks broadcast on radio.

The traders went on strike on Monday demanding that the government scrap a new 17 percent Value Added Tax (VAT) levied on all processed goods and return instead to the 15 percent Commercial Transaction Levy (CTL) which VAT replaced.
The new tax took effect on July 1 this year.

Opposition politician Ken Lukyamuzi was held briefly by police on Thursday but was released after questioning, his family said. On Friday police also set free a radio presenter with a private station arrested on Thursday on charges he was inciting the striking traders to persist with their action.
Police stepped up their presence in major towns after traders threatened to force fuel stations to close as well.
In Kampala small pockets of traders sat at street corners outside their shops chatting. Armed policemen kept watch.

Most of the streets in the capital were deserted and only markets selling food items, offices and banks were open for business. The striking traders threatened to loot shops defying their order to close.
Finance minister Jehoash Mayanja-Nkangi has said he will not review the tax, saying Uganda would lose up to a billion shillings ($910,000) for each percentage point reduction in the tax.
Museveni was due to meet his cabinet later on Friday to try and end the industrial action, which is costing his government three billion shillings in possible revenue daily.
Prices for consumer goods such as sugar, milk, eggs, agricultural produce and a range of others rose by between 20 and 50 percent, shoppers said.
